questions.prompt: Version 2 of your service starts writing a new `phone` field. The v1 servers still running in your rolling upgrade must handle records that contain it. Which property do the v1 servers need?
options: Backward compatibility
Forward compatibility
Serializability
Idempotence

questions.prompt: In Protocol Buffers, what identifies a field in the encoded bytes?
options: The field's name
Its position in the schema
Its tag number
A hash of its name and type

questions.prompt: You add `string phone = 4;` to a Protocol Buffers schema. Can old code read messages that include it?
options: No: old code fails on tags it doesn't recognize
Yes: old code skips fields with tags it doesn't know
Only if the field is marked required
Only after the old code is recompiled with the new schema

questions.prompt: Field 3 (`nickname`, a string) is no longer needed. What should you do with tag 3?
options: Reuse it for the next new field so tags stay compact
Reuse it, but only for another string field
Remove the field and reserve tag 3 so it's never used again
Keep the field forever and mark it required

questions.prompt: Avro encodings contain no field names or tag numbers. How does a reader know which bytes belong to which field?
options: Every Avro value starts with its field name
It resolves the writer's schema against its own reader's schema, matching fields by name
Fields must always appear in alphabetical order
It guesses from the byte patterns

questions.prompt: In Avro, which change keeps a schema both forward and backward compatible?
options: Adding a field that has a default value
Adding a field without a default value
Renaming a field without adding an alias
Changing a field from a string to an int

questions.prompt: Your JavaScript frontend parses JSON API responses. Tweet ids are 64-bit integers like 1234567890123456789. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; JSON numbers are arbitrary precision
JSON can't encode numbers that large at all
JavaScript numbers are 64-bit floats, so ids above 2⁵³ silently lose precision
The ids are converted to strings automatically

questions.prompt: An old version of your app reads a row, changes one field, and writes the whole row back. A newer version had added a `preferences` field to that row. What's the risk?
options: None; the database rejects the old app's write
The old app silently drops `preferences` when it writes the row back
The new app can no longer read the row
The row is duplicated
